title: Jensen Huang Says AI Will Create More Jobs, Not Fewer. For India’s Six Million Tech Workers, the Argument Is Personal.
excerpt: At Dell Technologies World and Carnegie Mellon’s commencement, the Nvidia CEO laid out a vision where AI demand is going parabolic — and insisted software engineers are busier than ever.
body:
Every week brings another headline about AI replacing jobs. Last week, it was Meta cutting 8,000 positions. This week, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang stepped onto stages in Las Vegas and Pittsburgh to make the opposite case — and his argument, backed by the most valuable chipmaker on earth, carries unusual weight.

At Dell Technologies World on May 19, Huang declared that AI demand is “utterly parabolic,” projecting three to four trillion dollars in global AI spending by 2030. A day earlier, at Carnegie Mellon University’s 128th commencement ceremony, he told graduates their careers were beginning “at the start of the AI revolution” and urged them to “shape what comes next.”

## The Core Argument

Huang’s thesis is not complicated: every time a technology dramatically lowers the cost of creating something, the world creates far more of that something. AI is making software cheaper to produce, but rather than eliminating programmers, it is generating an explosion in demand. “Software engineers are busier than ever,” he said. “The amount of software that needs to be written has expanded enormously.”

He pointed to radiology as a concrete example. AI diagnostic tools have not replaced radiologists — they have created a surge in the volume of scans hospitals process, which in turn demands more human expertise to interpret edge cases and manage patient care. The same logic, Huang argued, applies across every knowledge profession.

## The India Connection

For the estimated six million technology workers in India — and several hundred thousand Indian-origin engineers in Silicon Valley — Huang’s argument is not academic. Meta’s layoffs this week disproportionately affected its Indian workforce. Infosys, Wipro, and TCS have all flagged AI-driven productivity gains that allow them to deliver the same output with fewer bodies. The Indian IT services model, built on labour arbitrage, faces its most serious structural threat since cloud computing.

Huang’s counter-narrative offers some comfort, but it requires a crucial assumption: that displaced workers can be retrained fast enough to fill the new roles AI creates. India’s current educational infrastructure offers mixed evidence. The Azim Premji University’s 2026 report revealed that 40 per cent of Indian graduates remain unemployed, with even IIT alumni struggling to find placements. If the existing system cannot place graduates in traditional roles, the transition to AI-native ones will be steeper still.

## Nvidia’s Own Bet

Huang is not merely philosophising — Nvidia has committed over $90 billion in 2026 to AI infrastructure, including partnerships with Corning to build optical connectivity in Texas and North Carolina that will create 3,000 manufacturing jobs. A separate deal with Dell positions Nvidia’s Vera CPUs as the backbone of enterprise AI, with 5,000-plus companies already using the Dell AI Factory platform.

The Nvidia CEO also addressed China, stating he believes Beijing will “eventually reopen” its market to American AI chips despite current export restrictions. For India’s semiconductor ambitions — the Modi government has pledged $10 billion to build domestic chip fabrication — the geopolitics of AI hardware supply chains remains directly relevant.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

Indian-origin tech professionals occupy a unique vantage point in this debate. Many work at the very companies building AI tools, while simultaneously watching those tools restructure the Indian services firms where their careers began. Sundar Pichai at Google, Satya Nadella at Microsoft, and Arvind Krishna at IBM are each navigating the tension between AI-driven efficiency and workforce obligations.

Huang’s optimism is backed by Nvidia’s staggering Q1 revenue of $79 billion — a 79 per cent increase — but his argument requires a world where policy, education, and corporate investment align to make the transition work. For India’s tech workforce, the question is not whether AI creates jobs in the aggregate, but whether those jobs arrive in the same places and at the same pace as the ones that vanish.
